utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-16-T, the Prosecutor versus Zoran Kupreskic, Mirjan Kupreskic, Vlatko Kupreskic, Drago Josipovic, Dragan Papic, Vladimir Santic, also known as "Vlado."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. Good morning. Before we start, may I say that yesterday, I realised that Mr. Josipovic had some difficulty in looking at the witness and had to move backwards, probably because of the pillar. I think it is a basic and fundamental right of the accused to take a look at the witness so that he can afterwards confer with his Defence counsel. So this morning I checked with an officer early in the morning, and we realised that actually from there, if you sit and want to take notes, you can't see the witness. So I asked whether arrangements could be made so that you can -- probably that table can be moved a little bit so you, Mr Josipovic, don't have any difficulty in looking at the witness. But I hope that at lunch time measures will be taken, and if you have any problem, please let me know. Yes, Counsel Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJINA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Mr. President, yesterday I failed to give you a precise answer as to when the videotape was taken exactly, the videotape that was shown yesterday in the courtroom. The videotape was filmed on the 18th of March, 1998, in Ahmici, and we informed the Prosecutor of the date in the letter that we sent him accompanying the videotape. I have a written statement of the individual which appears on the videotape which was given on the same day that the tape was filmed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Counsel Krajina. Mr. Terrier?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Court expressed the wish to have the Prosecutor express her views in relation to a motion filed in relation to the Cerkez and Kordic proceedings. We were going to speak about that during the course of the day. We are ready to state our views to the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the time you need to do so. Could that be dealt with quite quickly? How long do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: Five minutes. It won't take very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Well, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TERRIER
utterances.text: I would like to state that this motion filed by counsel for Kordic and Cerkez requires disclosure of testimonies done in closed session before the Court and the filing of exhibits filed under seal. The Defence of both accused is based on Article 20 of the Statute which guarantees the rights, fundamental rights, of the Defence, it maintains the needs expressed by the Defence as well as an order for protective measures issued by the Trial Chamber on the 27th of January which could be notified and extended to statements which would have to be filed pursuant to such a motion. We want to state that according to the practice established by this Trial Chamber, to the extent possible, the principle of the publicity of our hearings has been adhered to, has been respected. We only move to closed sessions when there was a problem related to the possible identification of a protected witness, so this is very restricted when you see everything that has been made available and everything that has been done during these hearings. The second argument I would like to put forward is as follows: As far as I know, in the Kordic-Cerkez case, there has been no disclosure based on Rule 66; therefore, the request filed to you is of a very general nature. It relates to all statements or testimonies made in closed sessions and all statements under seal. The very general nature of this motion creates a problem; indeed, if such a motion was to be granted. Irrelevant testimonies, when it comes to the Defence of the accused Kordic and Cerkez, would be disclosed. Therefore, I have the feeling that today, given the state of the proceedings instituted against Kordic and Cerkez, this request is premature. If, later, in the course of the proceedings, the Defence was able to specify its request, I would have absolutely no objection. It would even be necessary for such statements under seal and such exhibits under seal to be disclosed. But given the very general nature of the present motion, it creates a problem. If it related to relevant testimonies for the Defence, it would not be a problem at all. But as it is, it seems to be premature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If I could ask Counsel Pavkovic whether he is also in a position to set out the position of the Defence on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. The Defence has reviewed the motion filed by the Defence counsel of Cerkez, and we agree that all the material from the sessions can be placed at the disposal of the Defence counsel if they feel that this is beneficial to them in preparing their Defence cases. Therefore, we are not opposed to their demand; we support it. Whether they need this material or not, that is up to them to assess. But as the Prosecution has stated, we don't think that anything need be specified, so whether they be informed of this today is a question of their Defence strategy. When we are talking about them, it is a very serious case, so I think that all the material should be sent to them on time, today. Because of the character of the hearings, because it was a public hearing, this was not accessible to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you, Counsel Pavkovic. However, the Prosecutor made two points: First, the request is extremely general and sweeping; and second, it is premature. So therefore, the Prosecutor suggested that we might put off any decision on this matter to see how the proceedings are going on and so on. What is your stand on this particular point? You may agree that the request is very general, of course, but what about the idea of it being premature?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, are you going to make a ruling now or are we going to put off this issue for some time? I think that the Defence position on this issue will always be the same. We don't want to enter into the question of whether it is premature or not. If the Defence counsel has asked for it, they probably have reasons for asking for it today, and I understand why they take this view. So whether it is general or not, that question I think can also be answered in the following way: We support the opinions of our colleagues. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. So we will decide on this matter in due course, and in light of the views that have been set forth by the Prosecutor and the Defence, we can now -- we are grateful to you for being so concise and to-the-point, and let us now move on to our next witness. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Good morning. Could you please stand and read the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: This witness has requested name, voice, and face protection, and at this time, I hand to the usher a slip of paper which is the Prosecution's next exhibit, 200, I believe.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 200.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I would ask the witness to look at that slip of paper and, without reading it, indicate whether that is his name, and if it's misspelled or if it's not his correct name, to say so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Moskowitz, could you let us know the name in each case, please? When we've got these pseudonyms, it's important to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This would be Witness Q. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness Q.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I am going to ask, as you speak, to try to do so in that microphone and to do so as clearly as you can. Just to let you know, you have been granted the protection measures that you have requested and so you should know that your name, your face, and your voice have been protected, and therefore you can feel confident in providing full and complete testimony to this Tribunal today. Do you have any questions about what I have said so far?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: You should also know that if there comes a time during your testimony that we will need to discuss matters, such as the names of certain individuals or to discuss certain places on a map that might tend to give away your identity, that at that time we will ask the Tribunal to go into what is known as closed session, and what that means, as I have already explained to you previously, what that means is that your voice will not leave this room, and therefore you can, at those times, also feel confident to be very candid with the Tribunal and to give us the benefit of your memory in the most complete way that you can. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Or do you have any questions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: No, I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Are you ready to begin your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Just to begin, could you tell us what year you were born in or what your age is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was born in 1945. I am 53 years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Up to 1993, where did you live?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How long had you lived in Ahmici?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I was born in Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you give us a little bit of an idea of how much education you've had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I am a chemical worker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Where did you work back in those days in 1993 and before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: In the Vitezit work organisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: How much schooling have you had? How many years of school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I have completed eight years of primary school and three years of a craft school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us generally what part of the village of Ahmici you lived in in the years before 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: I lived in the lower part in Ahmici, in front of the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you can, who some of your closest Croatian neighbours were during those times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: Yes, I can. There was Dragan Vidovic, Milka Vidovic, Mirko Vidovic, Vlatko Kupreskic. Those were my closest neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Now, without naming any names, could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Moskowitz. Counsel Puliselic would like to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PULISELIC
utterances.text: If the witness could move closer to the microphone so we could hear him better? If he could move closer to the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: The witness may wish to speak a little bit louder. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Yes. Witness Q, if you could speak up just a little bit so that everyone here in the room can hear you? Without naming any names, tell us generally the composition of your own immediate family during the time period of 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS Q
utterances.text: My family was as follows: I had four children and a wife and myself and a mother and father and three brothers and two sisters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: We apologise, Mr. President, but we can't hear anything again. (Discussion with registrar about technical problems)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand because of voice distortion it's very difficult to -- I mean, adjust the technical equipment, but probably the witness should try to speak up and speak a bit louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, on Channel 6, we have no transmission. We hear nothing on Channel 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Perhaps Channel 7 might work better. Have you tried that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAVKOVIC
utterances.text: Then on Channel 7, we don't hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I understand you should try Channel 7. Let us hope that you can hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I apologise, Witness Q. There have been some technical problems with the microphone, but I think now we can proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. SLOKOVIC-GLUMAC
utterances.text: We don't have translation on Channel 7. We don't have translation into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: I hesitate to make this suggestion because I think we've had too many, perhaps, closed sessions, but much of this testimony may have to be in closed session because it deals with houses. I think maybe afterward we can see how much really can be released to the public in terms of a transcript, but if we go into closed session, then I think that would take care of the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: No voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOSKOWITZ
utterances.text: Then we don't need voice distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: I think it is a very good suggestion. So we will move into closed session so that we have no voice distortion. Probably you can hear better. And on what Channel?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Channel 6, if Your Honour ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: Channel 6. So we move into closed session. (Closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CASSESE
utterances.text: 5.00 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 24th day of September, 1998, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: Page 2745 to 2862 redacted - in closed session
